edits.before: Conformal prediction provides a framework for calibrating prediction sets or bounds using held-out conformity scores under stated assumptions [5]. SAFE-Pipe uses grouped calibration residuals to construct a one-sided upper runtime estimate. Its small, fixed-profile evaluation is not evidence of universal coverage. Candidate selection, changes of input profile and changes of hardware require their own assessment; a nominal calibration target is not automatically a job-success probability.
edits.after: Conformal prediction calibrates prediction sets or bounds using held-out scores. Its usual marginal coverage argument requires exchangeability of calibration and future scores [5]. SAFE-Pipe computes one maximum residual score per family/configuration group. Keeping repeats together prevents repeat leakage, but does not establish exchangeability across the fixed groups, new profiles or different hardware. The nominal level is therefore reported alongside observed coverage; it is not a selected-job success probability [8].

edits.before: LightGBM predicts log successful engine runtime using 120 trees, seven leaves, learning rate 0.05, minimum child count three and L2 penalty one. Calibration uses the maximum log residual over each group’s repetitions. The nominal 90% finite-sample rank over 12 calibration groups selects the largest calibration score. The stored upper log offset is 0.523642, giving U = t * exp(0.523642), approximately 1.688 * t. The prediction and calibration components follow the methodological background in [4] and [5]. [7]
edits.after: LightGBM fits log successful engine runtime with 120 trees, seven leaves, learning rate 0.05, minimum child count three, L2 penalty one, seed 2026 and one training thread. Family and configuration ID are one-hot encoded. Calibration takes the maximum log residual per family/configuration group. With 12 groups and alpha 0.1, the finite-sample rank selects the largest score. The stored log offset 0.523642 gives U = t * exp(0.523642), approximately 1.688 * t [8].

edits.before: The saved artifact contains held-out predictions and metrics; an iteration-wise training history was not retained. The reported metrics use the saved model without retraining. Figures 5 and 6 use the saved test predictions.
edits.after: LightGBM is the fixed tabular regression model. The recorded comparison uses a family-median baseline, not alternative learned models. No archived tuning or sensitivity study establishes the 120-tree/seven-leaf settings as optimal, and no iteration-wise training history was retained. Figures 5 and 6 use saved held-out predictions without retraining [8, 9].

edits.before: The grouped split keeps all repetitions of a family/configuration pair together. edits.before: The original model is supported by only four fixed profiles, and its test contains eight family/configuration groups. Research uses one generation seed and shared samples. Runtime repetitions are not independent new workloads. Some costs are historical replays, not online executions; resource terms are configured proxies. Worker death and snapshot timing can censor telemetry. No cross-machine generalization, AWS Glue evaluation, multi-node experiment, calibrated failure classifier or publishable novel selector is established by these records.
edits.after: The original model is supported by only four fixed profiles, and its test contains eight family/configuration groups. Research uses one generation seed and shared samples. Runtime repeats are not independent new workloads; grouping them does not establish exchangeability across calibration and future workloads. The model settings and balanced weights were not shown to be optimal by a sensitivity study. Some costs are historical replays, not online executions, and resource terms are configured proxies. Worker death and snapshot timing can censor telemetry. These records do not establish cross-machine generalization, AWS Glue performance, multi-node performance, a calibrated failure classifier or a generally superior selector.
